# EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven
Coding Systems

Wentao Zhang1,† ,\mathpunct{,} Jianfeng Wang2,† ,\mathpunct{,} Liheng Liang3,†
,\mathpunct{,} Yilei Zhao1 ,\mathpunct{,} HaiBin Wen4 ,\mathpunct{,} Zhe
Zhao5,‡  
1 Nanyang Technological University 2 East China University of Science and
Technology  
3 Guangdong Ocean University 4 City University of Hong Kong 5 Stanford
University  
zhangwent963@gmail.com, ehz0002@stanford.edu

###### Abstract.

As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in programming tasks, LLM-
driven coding systems have evolved from one-shot code generation into complex
systems capable of iterative improvement during inference. However, existing
code benchmarks primarily emphasize static correctness and implicitly assume
fixed model capability during inference. As a result, they do not capture
inference-time self-evolution, such as whether accuracy and efficiency improve
as an agent iteratively refines its solutions. They also provide limited
accounting of resource costs and rarely calibrate model performance against
that of human programmers. Moreover, many benchmarks are dominated by high-
resource languages, leaving cross-language robustness and long-tail language
stability underexplored. Therefore, we present EvoCodeBench, a benchmark for
evaluating self-evolving LLM-driven coding systems across programming
languages with direct comparison to human performance. EvoCodeBench tracks
performance dynamics, measuring solution correctness alongside efficiency
metrics such as solving time, memory consumption, and improvement algorithmic
design over repeated problem-solving attempts. To ground evaluation in a
human-centered reference frame, we directly compare model performance with
that of human programmers on the same tasks, enabling relative performance
assessment within the human ability distribution. Furthermore, EvoCodeBench
supports multiple programming languages, enabling systematic cross-language
and long-tail stability analyses under a unified protocol. Our results
demonstrate that self-evolving systems exhibit measurable gains in efficiency
over time, and that human-relative and multi-language analyses provide
insights unavailable through accuracy alone. EvoCodeBench establishes a
foundation for evaluating coding intelligence in evolving LLM-driven systems.

Performance Comparison, Programming Languages

##  1\. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have progressed from code-completion utilities to
general-purpose programming assistants and building blocks for agentic coding
systems. In contrast to one-shot code generation, contemporary agents can
_self-evolve_ during inference by iteratively refining candidate programs,
repairing failures using execution feedback, and reusing intermediate
artifacts, tools, or memory to improve both correctness and efficiency within
the same problem-solving process. This shift motivates a central evaluation
challenge: how should coding competence be measured when behavior is adaptive
at inference time and performance is jointly determined by solution quality,
resource cost, and improvement dynamics? Early benchmarks such as HumanEval
(Chen, [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib1 "Evaluating large
language models trained on code")), MBPP (Austin et al.,
[2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib2 "Program synthesis with
large language models")), and APPS (Hendrycks et al.,
[2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib16 "Measuring coding
challenge competence with apps")) standardized evaluation by measuring
functional correctness via unit tests under fixed specifications, while
competition-level datasets such as CodeContests (Li et al.,
[2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib17 "Competition-level code
generation with alphacode")) further raised the difficulty ceiling. Subsequent
work strengthened test suites (Liu et al.,
[2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib18 "Is your code generated
by chatgpt really correct? rigorous evaluation of large language models for
code generation")), increased freshness via continuously updated algorithmic
tasks (LiveCodeBench (Jain et al.,
[2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib3 "Livecodebench: holistic
and contamination free evaluation of large language models for code"))), and
addressed repository-level software engineering settings (SWE-Bench (Jimenez
et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib4 "Swe-bench: can
language models resolve real-world github issues?"))), while recent extensions
broaden coverage across languages and incorporate efficiency-oriented signals
such as execution cost and resource overhead (Raihan et al.,
[2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib5 "MHumanEval-a multilingual
benchmark to evaluate large language models for code generation"); Xu et al.,
[2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib6 "Cruxeval-x: a benchmark
for multilingual code reasoning, understanding and execution"); Qing et al.,
[2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib7 "EffiBench-x: a multi-
language benchmark for measuring efficiency of llm-generated code"); Huang et
al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib24 "Effibench:
benchmarking the efficiency of automatically generated code")). However, a
coherent framework for evaluating inference-time self-evolution in coding
agents remains underdeveloped.

Despite these advances, existing benchmarks exhibit three limitations when
applied to LLM-based coding systems, including one-shot models and agentic
systems that self-evolve during inference. First, the prevailing paradigm
remains static and benchmarks treat problems as independent one-shot instances
and score systems primarily by final correctness, which obscures inference-
time dynamics. Recent methods such as Self-Refine (Madaan et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib21 "Self-refine: iterative
refinement with self-feedback, 2023")) and Reflexion (Shinn et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib22 "Reflexion: language
agents with verbal reinforcement learning, 2023")) demonstrate that iterative
refinement can substantially boost pass rates, yet existing benchmarks rarely
quantify whether a system becomes more accurate and efficient within the
inference process, how quickly it improves as it refines solutions, or what
time and memory costs are incurred, so they cannot distinguish fast, reliable
solvers from systems that succeed only after expensive trial-and-error
(Olausson et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib23 "Is
self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?")). Second, results are
typically reported in absolute accuracy units with limited calibration to
human performance. Without human-referenced metrics, it is difficult to
interpret what a given pass rate implies about practical coding competence or
to report where a system falls on a human-calibrated scale, including its
percentile rank or the number of humans it outperforms on the same tasks.
Third, multilingual coverage is often dominated by a single language and
ecosystem (often Python), which can mask cross-language generalization and
bias evaluation toward familiar tooling and idioms. Although multilingual
benchmarks such as MultiPL-E (Cassano et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib19 "Multipl-e: a scalable
and polyglot approach to benchmarking neural code generation")) have extended
evaluation to many languages, they still lack efficiency and human-referential
metrics. This imbalance is especially problematic under long-tail usage
patterns. According to the TIOBE Index for January 2026, Python accounts for
22.61% and Kotlin accounts for 0.97% (TIOBE Software BV,
[2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib15 "TIOBE index")). Such
market skew can translate into differences in the amount of training data
available per language, potentially inducing systematic bias in LLMs, yet
existing benchmarks rarely measure or diagnose this effect.

We introduce EvoCodeBench to address these gaps with an evaluation framework
for LLM-driven coding systems, including both one-shot models and self-
evolving agents. EvoCodeBench evaluates systems on competitive-programming-
style problems in multiple mainstream languages (e.g., Python, C++, Java, Go,
and Kotlin), and it is designed to capture inference-time improvement rather
than only final outcomes. Beyond pass rate, EvoCodeBench records efficiency
and resource usage signals, including wall-clock solving time, memory
consumption, and improvement trajectories as the system solves problems during
inference. We pair these measurements with platform-side judging in a
standardized execution environment, which returns acceptance status and fine-
grained performance feedback such as runtime, memory usage, and percentile-
based _beats_ statistics, enabling analyses of whether gains in correctness
come with disproportionate cost. We also provide standardized evaluation
scripts and reporting templates to facilitate reproducibility and fair
comparisons across model families and agent configurations. Finally,
EvoCodeBench enables human-referenced reporting by situating model performance
within the distribution of human submissions on the same tasks, including
percentile ranks and the number of human solutions a system outperforms.
Specifically, we make the following contributions:

    * •

We present the first systematic, human-referenced evaluation of LLM-based
coding systems, situating model performance within the empirical distribution
of human submissions and enabling interpretable comparisons in terms of
percentile rank and the number of humans a system outperforms.

    * •

We reformulate coding evaluation from a static, endpoint-focused paradigm to a
trajectory-level analysis that jointly characterizes correctness, efficiency,
and resource cost during inference-time self-evolution, and we empirically
validate the necessity and stability of this evaluation framework across
multiple languages, including long-tail programming ecosystems.

    * •

We release EvoCodeBench, a large-scale multilingual benchmark with
standardized judging, human baselines, and reproducible evaluation protocols,
and demonstrate how its metrics provide actionable insights for the design and
future development of coding LLMs and agentic systems.

##  2\. Related Work

###  2.1. Evaluating LLMs on Isolated Coding Tasks

Early benchmarks for evaluating LLMs on programming tasks primarily emphasize
static correctness on small, self-contained problems. Representative datasets
such as HumanEval (Chen, [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib1
"Evaluating large language models trained on code")) and MBPP (Austin et al.,
[2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib2 "Program synthesis with
large language models")) assess whether a generated function satisfies a
predefined specification by passing a fixed suite of unit tests, while APPS
(Hendrycks et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib16
"Measuring coding challenge competence with apps")) and CodeContests (Li et
al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib17 "Competition-level
code generation with alphacode")) raise the difficulty ceiling to competitive-
programming-level challenges with thousands of problems. Subsequent variants
with strengthened test suites, including HumanEval Pro and MBPP Pro (Yu et
al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib8 "Humaneval pro and
mbpp pro: evaluating large language models on self-invoking code generation"))
and EvalPlus (Liu et al.,
[2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib18 "Is your code generated
by chatgpt really correct? rigorous evaluation of large language models for
code generation")), further tighten correctness criteria to better
discriminate among strong models. These benchmarks have played a central role
in standardizing evaluation protocols for functional code generation and
tracking rapid progress in model capabilities.

However, these evaluations largely assume fixed model behavior during
inference and treat each problem as an independent one-shot instance.
Consequently, they provide limited visibility into inference-time self-
evolution, even though methods such as Self-Refine (Madaan et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib21 "Self-refine: iterative
refinement with self-feedback, 2023")) and Reflexion (Shinn et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib22 "Reflexion: language
agents with verbal reinforcement learning, 2023")) have shown that iterative
refinement can substantially improve pass rates, and analyses of self-repair
(Olausson et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib23 "Is
self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?")) highlight the need to
account for computational cost when evaluating such gains. To address concerns
about data contamination and task realism, later benchmarks such as
LiveCodeBench (Jain et al.,
[2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib3 "Livecodebench: holistic
and contamination free evaluation of large language models for code")) curate
continuously updated algorithmic problems sourced from competitive programming
platforms and evaluate auxiliary skills such as self-repair and test-output
prediction. Despite improvements in data freshness and diversity, the dominant
paradigm remains centered on final correctness on fixed tasks and offers
limited calibration to human performance or systematic characterization of
inference-time efficiency dynamics.

###  2.2. Benchmarking LLM-Driven Coding Systems

Beyond isolated function synthesis, recent work has increasingly shifted
toward evaluating LLM-based agents and more complex coding systems in
realistic software engineering settings. Repository-level benchmarks assess a
model’s ability to resolve real-world issues through multi-file code edits,
dependency reasoning, and test-driven validation, marking an important step
toward capturing practical workflows (Jimenez et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib4 "Swe-bench: can language
models resolve real-world github issues?"); Liu et al.,
[2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib14 "Repobench: benchmarking
repository-level code auto-completion systems")). Class-level benchmarks such
as ClassEval (Du et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib27
"Evaluating large language models in class-level code generation")) move
beyond function-level evaluation to assess generation of interdependent code
units, while broader task suites like BigCodeBench (Zhuo et al.,
[2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib26 "Bigcodebench:
benchmarking code generation with diverse function calls and complex
instructions")) evaluate diverse function-call composition across libraries.
In parallel, agent-oriented benchmarks investigate multi-step reasoning, tool
use, and interaction (Liu et al.,
[2023c](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib9 "Agentbench: evaluating
llms as agents"); Guo et al.,
[2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib10 "Stabletoolbench: towards
stable large-scale benchmarking on tool learning of large language models");
Mialon et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib11 "Gaia: a
benchmark for general ai assistants"); Yao et al.,
[2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib12 "τ-Bench: a benchmark for
tool-agent-user interaction in real-world domains")), and multi-agent
frameworks such as MapCoder (Islam et al.,
[2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib25 "Mapcoder: multi-agent
code generation for competitive problem solving")) demonstrate that
decomposing the code generation pipeline into specialized agents can improve
competitive-programming performance.

More recent extensions expand evaluation along additional dimensions such as
multilingual coverage and efficiency awareness by examining cross-language
generalization (Cassano et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib19 "Multipl-e: a scalable
and polyglot approach to benchmarking neural code generation"); Ding et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib20 "Crosscodeeval: a diverse
and multilingual benchmark for cross-file code completion"); Raihan et al.,
[2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib5 "MHumanEval-a multilingual
benchmark to evaluate large language models for code generation"); Xu et al.,
[2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib6 "Cruxeval-x: a benchmark
for multilingual code reasoning, understanding and execution")) and
incorporating execution cost, runtime performance, or memory overhead into
evaluation protocols (Huang et al.,
[2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib24 "Effibench: benchmarking
the efficiency of automatically generated code"); Qing et al.,
[2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib7 "EffiBench-x: a multi-
language benchmark for measuring efficiency of llm-generated code")). However,
these extensions primarily add new axes without fundamentally revising the
underlying evaluation target. Even when efficiency signals are reported, they
are rarely integrated with inference-time adaptation and improvement dynamics,
and multilingual coverage is often dominated by high-resource languages,
leaving long-tail stability underexplored.

###  2.3. Limitations of Existing Benchmarks

Across both isolated coding benchmarks and agent-oriented evaluation
frameworks, a common limitation persists. Even as state-of-the-art models
approach performance saturation on strengthened algorithmic benchmarks (e.g.,
HumanEval Pro and MBPP Pro) and demonstrate competitive results on realistic
software engineering tasks (e.g., SWE-Bench subsets), there is no established
framework that jointly measures inference-time self-evolution, efficiency, and
human-relative capability. In particular, existing benchmarks provide limited
human-referenced metrics, which constrains the interpretability of claims
about human-level or superhuman coding ability. Moreover, they do not
explicitly characterize whether systems become faster or more accurate during
inference as they refine solutions (Madaan et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib21 "Self-refine: iterative
refinement with self-feedback, 2023"); Shinn et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib22 "Reflexion: language
agents with verbal reinforcement learning, 2023")), nor do they systematically
link such improvements to time and memory costs. Finally, language coverage
remains skewed toward high-resource languages, and market-level usage skew can
translate into training-data imbalance and language bias (TIOBE Software BV,
[2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib15 "TIOBE index")), yet
benchmarks rarely quantify this effect. These gaps motivate the need for an
evaluation framework that jointly models performance dynamics, efficiency,
human-relative capability, and cross-language stability, which we address in
EvoCodeBench.

##  3\. EvoCodeBench

###  3.1. Benchmark Design Rationale

Our benchmark construction is driven by the three motivations outlined above,
namely evaluating inference-time self-evolution, calibrating performance
against human ability, and assessing cross-language robustness under long-tail
language usage. To this end, we build EvoCodeBench on top of the LeetCode
online judge, which provides an execution-based evaluation interface and rich
feedback signals that closely match our requirements. Specifically, acceptance
status and pass rate, together with the number of passed test cases for
partially correct submissions, enable fine-grained assessment of functional
correctness beyond binary success. For accepted submissions, the platform
reports runtime and memory usage, along with percentile-based runtime beats
and memory beats statistics computed against the distribution of human
submissions, which directly supports human-referenced evaluation. Finally,
LeetCode provides standardized starter code across many programming languages,
enabling consistent multi-language evaluation and the study of long-tail
language stability under a unified measurement protocol. These signals also
facilitate analyzing efficiency–accuracy trade-offs and identifying failure
modes that emerge only under constrained runtime or memory budgets.

###  3.2. Benchmark Construction

Data Collection. We collect problems through the SQL interface provided by
LeetCode and retrieve the full set of 3,822 programming problems available at
the time of crawling. For each problem, we extract the full natural-language
statement and normalize it into a structured representation that preserves key
semantic elements, including embedded images when present, as well as the
official input–output examples. We store image links and resolve them to local
assets so that models can be evaluated with the same visual context as human
solvers. In addition, we collect language-specific starter code templates for
a broad set of languages, enabling consistent prompt construction and fair
cross-language comparison. Each problem is further annotated with its
platform-provided difficulty label (Easy, Medium, and Hard) and a set of
topical tags that describe the required algorithmic concepts and data
structures, such as arrays, trees, dynamic programming, mathematics, and
strings. During ingestion, we perform basic quality checks, including
filtering malformed records, removing duplicates, and validating that problem
statements, examples, and templates are successfully parsed. Figure
[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.3. Limitations of
Existing Benchmarks ‣ 2. Related Work ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance
Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems") summarizes tag and
difficulty distributions, used to guide dataset balancing and analyze
performance variation across problem categories and difficulty strata.

Problem Characteristics. LeetCode-style algorithmic problems provide a
controlled yet demanding setting for evaluating coding competence in both one-
shot LLMs and LLM-based agents. Each task specifies explicit constraints and
input–output behavior that must be matched exactly, stressing instruction
following, edge-case coverage, and implementation fidelity under a fixed
interface. The breadth of tags and difficulty levels further tests algorithm
selection, data-structure proficiency, and complexity-aware reasoning, while
requiring robust translation from high-level ideas to executable code. Because
evaluation is execution-based, brittle solutions are reliably exposed through
concrete failures such as off-by-one errors, corner-case bugs, and language-
specific pitfalls. Standardized starter templates across languages enable
systematic cross-language comparisons, including robustness in long-tail
languages with distinct syntax and runtime characteristics. Finally, since
many problems admit within-inference refinement, this setting probes agentic
behaviors such as self-repair, hypothesis testing against examples, and
efficiency-aware optimization under runtime and memory budgets.

Problem Evaluation. We adopt a unified evaluation protocol that standardizes
model interaction with the execution environment through a lightweight vanllia
coding agent, enabling fair and reproducible comparison across foundation
models. For each problem instance, the agent presents a fixed input
representation to the model and deterministically extracts executable source
code from the model’s output. The code is then submitted to an official
execution-based judging service, which evaluates functional correctness on
hidden test cases and reports resource usage statistics. This design ensures
that all models are assessed under identical input formats, execution
conditions, and scoring criteria.

To capture inference-time self-evolution, we further introduce a self-evolving
coding agent that allows models to iteratively refine their solutions within a
single problem-solving episode. Under a fixed revision budget, the agent
supports multiple rounds of solution updates while keeping the task
specification, prompt structure, and evaluation interface unchanged. This
controlled setup enables direct comparison between one-shot generation and
inference-time adaptive refinement, isolating the effect of self-evolution
from confounding factors such as prompt variation or task reformulation.

###  3.3. Agent Construction

In the preceding section, we introduced a lightweight coding agent and a self-
evolving coding agent as two standardized evaluation interfaces for comparing
foundation models on EvoCodeBench. In this subsection, we detail how each
agent is constructed, including the prompting and output-format constraints,
deterministic code extraction, and the submission-and-feedback loop with the
online judge. We then describe the within-inference reflection–revision
procedure used by the self-evolving agent, enabling analysis under the same
task specification and scoring protocol.

Coding Agent. As illustrated in Appendix
[C.1.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#A3.SS1.SSS3 "C.1.3. Prompt Example
‣ C.1. Agent Construction Details ‣ Appendix C Case Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A
Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems"), the
coding agent is deliberately designed to be lightweight and minimally
augmented. It receives as input a standardized prompt consisting of the
problem statement and a language-specific starter template, and it instructs
the model to produce a format-constrained response with two explicit fields.
The reasoning field contains the model’s intermediate reasoning, while the
code field contains the final solution expressed in the provided template
format. The agent deterministically extracts the code field and submits it to
the online judge for execution-based evaluation. Importantly, this baseline
agent operates in a single-pass manner and does not incorporate external
memory, tool use, or iterative refinement. Both the prompting schema and the
output parsing rules are fixed across models, ensuring that observed
performance differences can be attributed to the underlying model capabilities
rather than agent-level augmentation or inference-time adaptation.

Self-evolving Coding Agent. To evaluate inference-time self-evolution, we
design a self-evolving coding agent that performs controlled, within-inference
refinement of solution code. Starting from an initial model-generated draft,
the agent iteratively improves the solution through a fixed-budget sequence of
reflection and revision steps within a single problem-solving episode. At each
iteration, the agent prompts the model to analyze its current solution and
identify potential failure modes, including unhandled corner cases, logical
errors, suboptimal complexity, or language-specific issues. Based on this
analysis, the model proposes targeted code revisions aimed at improving
correctness or efficiency. The updated solution is then resubmitted to the
online judge, and execution feedback is recorded. Crucially, only the solution
artifact is modified during self-evolution. The problem specification, prompt
schema, evaluation interface, and model parameters remain fixed, ensuring that
observed gains are attributable solely to inference-time refinement rather
than changes in task formulation or external augmentation. By constraining
refinement to a single inference episode with a fixed revision budget, this
agent enables systematic analysis of improvement trajectories in both
correctness and efficiency.

##  4\. Empirical Studies

###  4.1. Experimental Settings

Benchmark Settings. We construct the evaluation set by sampling 100 problems
from the full collection of 3,822 tasks, spanning diverse tag categories to
cover a broad range of algorithmic skills. We avoid evaluating on the full
pool because widely circulated LeetCode problems, particularly older ones, may
overlap with the training data of commonly used LLMs. Such overlap can inflate
measured performance and confound comparisons through memorization. We
therefore focus on a recent set of 100 problems as a held out test set to
reduce the risk of data leakage while preserving topical diversity. We
evaluate models in five programming languages. We include widely used
languages such as Python3, C++, Java, and Go, and we additionally include
Kotlin as a representative long tail language. This choice enables analysis of
cross-language robustness under skewed language popularity and quantifies
performance shifts when moving from high- to lower-resource settings.

LLMs Settings. We evaluate a set of frontier models, including deepseek-v3.2,
grok-4.1-fast, gemini-3-flash-preview, gemini-3-pro-preview, claude-
sonnet-4.5, claude-opus-4.5 and gpt-5.2. For all models, we enable reasoning
by default. The maximum number of generated tokens to 65,536 for each
response.

Agent Settings. We use the coding agent without additional agent level
constraints beyond the standardized prompting and parsing protocol. For the
self-evolving coding agent, we allow at most three reflection and revision
iterations per problem.

###  4.2. Evaluation Metrics

We report three groups of metrics that capture complementary aspects of coding
performance. First, capability metrics measure functional correctness and
failure modes under the judge constraints. Second, efficiency metrics
summarize runtime and memory cost for accepted submissions. Third, human
metrics quantify how often accepted submissions outperform the distribution of
human solutions in runtime and memory.

Coding capability metrics.

    * •

Pass Rate (PR): The number of problems that the model successfully passed all
test cases within the time and memory limits.

    * •

Time Limit Exceeded (TLE): The number of problems where the model’s solution
exceeded the allowed execution time limit.

    * •

Memory Limit Exceeded (MLE): The number of problems where the model’s solution
exceeded the allowed memory usage.

    * •

Compile Error (CE): The number of problems where the model’s generated code
failed to compile due to syntax errors.

    * •

Runtime Error (RE): The number of problems where the model’s solution
encountered a runtime error during execution.

    * •

Wrong Answer (WA): The number of problems where the model’s solution produced
incorrect output for the test cases.

    * •

Timeout (TO): The number of problems where the model failed to generate a
response within the specified timeout period.

    * •

Response Error (RpE): The number of problems where the model failed to return
a valid or parseable code response.

Coding efficiency metrics.

    * •

Average Runtime (AR): The average execution runtime in milliseconds of the
model’s accepted solutions across all problems.

    * •

Average Memory (AM): The average memory consumption in megabytes of the
model’s accepted solutions across all problems.

    * •

Average Passed Cases (APC): The average number of test cases that the model’s
solutions successfully passed before failure.

Human-referenced metrics.

    * •

Average Runtime Beats (ARB): The percentage of accepted solutions where the
model’s runtime performance beats other human submissions.

    * •

Average Memory Beats (AMB): The percentage of accepted solutions where the
model’s memory beats human submissions.

###  4.3. Overall Comparison of Models

Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation
Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark
for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems") and Figure
[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation
Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark
for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems") report the main results of
EvoCodeBench across languages. The results are analyzed along three
complementary dimensions: coding capability, efficiency, and human-referenced
comparison. The empirical analysis are as follows:

####  4.3.1. Comparison of Coding Capability

We begin by analyzing pass rates together with detailed error profiles across
programming languages, which jointly provide a diagnostic view of both
solution quality and language-level execution robustness under heterogeneous
constraints. In Figure [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F3 "Figure 3
‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-
Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems"), this
dimension corresponds to the first row, which plots within-inference pass-rate
trajectories as problems accumulate.

Finding 1. Model performance degrades systematically from high-resource to
long-tail languages, indicating limited robustness to language coverage.
gpt-5.2 consistently emerges as the strongest performer in high-resource
settings, achieving the highest pass rates in Python3, C++, Java, and Go, with
PR values of 84, 90, 91, and 90, respectively. Notably, it is the only model
to exceed a pass rate of 90 in Java. Figure
[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation
Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark
for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems") corroborates this advantage in
the first row by showing that gpt-5.2 sustains one of the highest PR
trajectories across these languages throughout the task sequence. However, its
performance degrades in the long-tail language Kotlin, where the pass rate
drops to 78. This degradation coincides with a sharp rise in compilation
errors, with CE increasing to 17. More broadly, the first-row trajectories
show that nearly all models experience a downward shift when moving from high-
resource languages to Kotlin, indicating a structural robustness gap that
persists even for top performers.

Finding 2. Performance degradation in second-tier models is primarily driven
by code-level errors rather than algorithmic misunderstanding. The three
models claude-4.5-opus, gemini-3-flash-preview, and gemini-3-pro-preview form
a competitive cluster that achieves pass rates primarily in the 70 to high-80
range across languages. Their performance gap relative to gpt-5.2 is small in
Python3 but becomes more pronounced in compiled languages. In these settings,
compilation errors increase noticeably, particularly in Go and Kotlin.
Importantly, wrong-answer rates within this tier remain relatively stable
across languages, which suggests that the dominant bottleneck is not a
wholesale collapse in algorithm selection. Instead, failures are better
explained by language-specific implementation friction, such as syntax
details, library and API usage, and toolchain constraints that prevent
otherwise plausible solutions from executing correctly. This highlights that
in compiled and long-tail languages, executability and correctness are tightly
coupled, and code-level robustness can dominate observed performance even when
high-level solution ideas are similar.

Finding 3. Evaluations restricted to high-resource languages can substantially
overestimate the true coding capability of some models. grok-4.1-fast
maintains pass rates in the high 60 to low 70 for Python3, C++, and Java, but
shows a marked decline in Go and Kotlin, with pass rates dropping to 69 and
62, respectively. This decline is accompanied by elevated compilation error
rates of 16 in Go and 22 in Kotlin. These results support the hypothesis that
long-tail languages expose weaknesses in code generation robustness that are
not apparent when evaluation is restricted to Python-centric benchmarks.

Finding 4. Algorithmic inefficiency emerges as a distinct failure mode that is
not captured by pass rate alone. The model claude-4.5-sonnet demonstrates
consistently low pass rates across all languages, hovering around the low 40.
In contrast to other models, its failures are dominated by time limit exceeded
errors rather than compilation or response errors, with TLE counts exceeding
35 in every language evaluated. This indicates that the model frequently
produces syntactically valid and executable code, but struggles to select or
implement algorithms that meet the required efficiency constraints. Such
behavior underscores the importance of explicitly separating functional
correctness from algorithmic efficiency in the evaluation of coding systems,
since execution-based benchmarks must account not only for whether a solution
is correct, but also for whether it meets the computational constraints for
practical deployment.

Finding 5. Severe output format violations in some models reveal weaknesses in
structured code generation. The model deepseek-v3.2 performs worst overall,
exhibiting severe response errors across all languages. RpE counts exceed 35
in every setting and are further compounded by substantial compilation errors
in C++, Java, and Go. These failures undermine execution-based evaluation and
reveal weaknesses in output format compliance and instruction adherence,
independent of algorithmic difficulty.

In conclusion, our results highlight that multilingual robustness, efficiency
under judge constraints, and structured output reliability are all first-order
factors for LLM-based coding systems. To improve performance, models should
strengthen long-tail language competence through targeted multilingual
training and toolchain-aware code generation that reduces compilation and
execution-blocking errors. They should incorporate explicit efficiency
reasoning and optimization to avoid time-limit failures, and adopt schema-
constrained decoding and validation to prevent response-format violations that
preclude execution-based evaluation. These directions are complementary and
directly motivated by the failure patterns exposed by EvoCodeBench, reflecting
practical limitations observed across languages and execution settings.

####  4.3.2. Comparison of Coding Efficiency

We next examine efficiency using the three columns in Table
[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation
Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark
for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems") that summarize average runtime,
average memory, and average passed cases. These metrics quantify the
computational cost of accepted solutions and the depth of progress when
solutions fail. In Figure [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F3
"Figure 3 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A
Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems"), the
second row plots cumulative runtime as tasks accumulate. Lower curves indicate
stronger end-to-end efficiency under the judge interface because time limit
exceeded outcomes incur penalties and therefore increase accumulated cost.

Finding 1. Differences in end-to-end efficiency are primarily driven by the
stability of solution executability. In the second row of Figure
[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation
Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark
for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems"), gpt-5.2 consistently maintains
the lowest or near-lowest cumulative runtime across all languages. This
reflects not only fast accepted solutions but, more importantly, a high
success rate with very few penalties from compilation or execution failures.
Models such as gemini-3-pro-preview, gemini-3-flash-preview, and
claude-4.5-opus initially track closely to the best-performing curve, but as
tasks accumulate, particularly in Go and Kotlin, cumulative differences
gradually emerge due to slightly lower executability, which results in more
frequent failure penalties. In contrast, claude-4.5-sonnet and deepseek-v3.2
show much steeper cumulative runtime growth, dominated by timeout penalties,
even when some solutions are relatively fast. These observations indicate that
stable end-to-end efficiency is primarily determined by the model’s ability to
reliably produce executable solutions, and cumulative runtime effectively
amplifies differences in executability across models.

Finding 2. Among high pass-rate models, conditional runtime and memory still
exhibit substantial implementation-level differences. Average runtime and
average memory are computed only over accepted submissions and therefore
characterize conditional efficiency among solved problems. Among higher pass-
rate models, gpt-5.2 achieves competitive runtimes in compiled languages, with
228.62 ms in C++, 160.32 ms in Java, and 162.16 ms in Go, while gemini-3-pro-
preview attains the lowest average runtime among the stronger models in
Python3 at 1112.49 ms. Memory exhibits a different structure. Java and C++
typically have larger memory footprints while Go is often lower and Kotlin
falls in between, reflecting runtime-system differences. Within a fixed
language, however, models still vary substantially in average memory,
suggesting that implementation choices such as data structure selection and
allocation patterns materially affect efficiency beyond correctness.

Finding 3. Failures are not homogeneous: average passed cases reveal the stage
at which solutions break down. Average passed cases tends to remain high for
frontier models across languages, indicating that many failures occur after
passing a large portion of hidden tests and are consistent with late-stage
corner cases. When response errors or severe compilation issues occur, average
passed cases can drop and indicates early breakdowns that prevent deep test
coverage. deepseek-v3.2 illustrates this behavior in Java where average passed
cases drops to 481.45, consistent with its unstable execution outcomes. This
metric is complementary to cumulative runtime because it helps explain whether
penalties arise from early pipeline failures or from solutions that are close
to acceptance but miss a small set of cases.

In conclusion, efficiency differences in EvoCodeBench are shaped by penalty-
accumulating runtime trajectories and by the conditional runtime, memory, and
failure depth of accepted and near-miss solutions. This suggests actionable
guidance for coding agents that goes beyond correctness. Agents should perform
complexity-aware planning before coding, apply targeted revisions that replace
high-cost approaches when time-limit signals appear, and explicitly trade off
runtime and memory via data-structure choices. When failures occur, average
passed cases help distinguish early breakdowns from late-stage corner-case
errors, enabling more efficient refinement under fixed budgets.

####  4.3.3. Comparison of Human-referenced Performance

We evaluate human-referenced efficiency with ARB and AMB, which correspond to
_average runtime beats_ and _average memory beats_ against the empirical
distribution of human submissions for the same problem and programming
language. In Figure [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣
4.2. Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-
Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems"), this
dimension corresponds to the third row, which tracks cumulative averages of
runtime beats and memory beats as tasks accumulate. The solid and dotted
trajectories therefore indicate whether competitiveness against humans is
stable over the task sequence, rather than being driven by a small subset of
early and easy problems.

Finding 1. Strong models sustain human-competitive efficiency across
languages, and this competitiveness persists over the task sequence. Across
languages, frontier models typically achieve ARB and AMB above 50, indicating
that their accepted solutions are often faster and more memory efficient than
a majority of human submissions. This pattern is most pronounced for gpt-5.2,
which maintains consistently strong third-row trajectories and reaches
particularly high values in Kotlin, with ARB 88.44 and AMB 83.12.
claude-4.5-opus, gemini-3-flash-preview, and gemini-3-pro-preview also attain
high beats in several languages, and their third-row curves remain relatively
stable as more tasks accumulate. This suggests that human-competitive
efficiency is not limited to a small number of easy problems, but is
maintained across a broader slice of the benchmark.

Finding 2. Human-referenced beats decouple conditional efficiency from
benchmark coverage. Because ARB and AMB are defined only for accepted
submissions, a model with low pass rate can still appear strong in beats if
its few successful solutions are unusually efficient. For example,
deepseek-v3.2 attains a low pass rate of 11 in C++, yet its accepted
submissions achieve ARB 73.11 and AMB 74.05. This selection effect is also
visible in the third row, where some trajectories remain moderate even when
the corresponding pass-rate curve is low. As a result, beats metrics quantify
_conditional_ efficiency among solved cases, while pass rate measures
_coverage_ , and the two should be interpreted jointly when comparing models.

Finding 3. The gap between runtime beats and memory beats reveals distinct
tradeoffs relative to human solutions. In some settings, models achieve much
higher ARB than AMB, indicating solutions that prioritize speed over memory
compared to human submissions. For instance, in Python3 gpt-5.2 attains ARB
68.06 but AMB 37.98, suggesting stronger relative runtime competitiveness than
memory competitiveness. In other settings, ARB and AMB are closer, indicating
more balanced efficiency. The solid and dotted third-row trajectories make
these tradeoffs visible as tasks accumulate, complementing absolute runtime
and memory statistics with an interpretable human-referenced scale.

In conclusion, ARB and AMB together with the third-row trajectories in Figure
[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation
Metrics ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark
for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems") show that human-competitive
efficiency can be sustained across tasks, yet it interacts with both benchmark
coverage and runtime–memory tradeoffs. This suggests practical guidance for
coding agents. Agents should optimize for beats only after securing
correctness, choose a speed–memory tradeoff matching problem constraints, and
report beats jointly with pass rate to avoid over-interpreting efficiency from
few accepted cases.

###  4.4. Evaluation for Self-Evolving Agents

Self-evolving coding agents aim to improve solution quality and efficiency
during a single inference process through iterative refinement. Existing code
benchmarks typically evaluate only the final submission and therefore provide
limited visibility into when and how such within-inference self-evolution
helps. EvoCodeBench supports a more fine-grained evaluation because it exposes
execution outcomes, partial progress signals, and efficiency statistics,
enabling trajectory-level analyses in addition to endpoint scores. In what
follows, we evaluate self-evolving agents from two complementary perspectives.
We first summarize overall performance using the same standardized metrics as
in the main results. We then study within-inference evolution trajectories
across reflection and revision steps to quantify improvement dynamics.

Coding capability. Table [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.T2 "Table
2 ‣ 4.4.1. Self-Evolving Performance ‣ 4.4. Evaluation for Self-Evolving
Agents ‣ 4. Empirical Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark
for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems") compares a vanilla coding agent
against an evolving variant for gemini-3-flash-preview. Across languages, the
evolving agent yields relative pass-rate improvements of 10.1 to 26.7 percent.
Figure [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4.1. Self-
Evolving Performance ‣ 4.4. Evaluation for Self-Evolving Agents ‣ 4. Empirical
Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-
Driven Coding Systems") corroborates this in the first row by showing
consistently higher pass-rate trajectories as tasks accumulate. The effect is
strongest in compiled languages, where pass rates reach 99 in C++ and 98 in
Java. These improvements are accompanied by broad reductions in execution
blocking errors. Compilation error, runtime error, timeout, and response error
frequently drop to zero, indicating that iterative refinement effectively
repairs format and tooling issues. Beyond executability, the evolving agent
also reduces algorithmic failures. Time limit exceeded and wrong answer counts
decrease substantially, suggesting that self reflection helps identify
inefficient approaches and missed corner cases. Overall, within inference
refinement can convert many near miss submissions into accepted solutions
under the same evaluation interface.

Coding efficiency. Efficiency metrics show that the evolving agent improves
runtime in every language, with average runtime decreasing by 7.8 percent in
Python3 and by 19.8 to 46.4 percent in compiled languages. In Figure
[4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4.1. Self-Evolving
Performance ‣ 4.4. Evaluation for Self-Evolving Agents ‣ 4. Empirical Studies
‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven
Coding Systems"), the second row confirms this trend, as the evolving agent
accumulates substantially lower cumulative runtime and the gap widens as tasks
accumulate. This pattern is consistent with reductions in time limit exceeded
errors and suggests that evolution often replaces suboptimal algorithms with
more efficient ones. Memory usage shows a mixed trend, decreasing in C++,
Java, and Go but increasing modestly in Python3 and Kotlin, plausibly because
the evolving agent introduces auxiliary data structures to ensure correctness
or improve speed. Average passed cases changes only slightly, indicating that
most gains come from turning partial solutions into fully accepted ones rather
than uniformly increasing partial progress.

Human-referenced comparison. Human-referenced metrics further suggest that
evolution improves human calibrated efficiency in most languages. In Figure
[4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4.1. Self-Evolving
Performance ‣ 4.4. Evaluation for Self-Evolving Agents ‣ 4. Empirical Studies
‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven
Coding Systems"), the third row shows that the evolving agent maintains higher
runtime-beats and memory-beats trajectories than the vanilla agent in most
settings, indicating sustained competitiveness against human submissions as
tasks accumulate. Consistent with Table
[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.4.1. Self-Evolving
Performance ‣ 4.4. Evaluation for Self-Evolving Agents ‣ 4. Empirical Studies
‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven
Coding Systems"), runtime beats increase strongly in compiled languages, with
ARB gains of 30.8 percent in C++ and 24.4 percent in Java, and smaller gains
in Go and Kotlin. Memory beats increase in Python3, C++, Java, and Go, but
decrease in Kotlin. This divergence mirrors the absolute memory trend and
suggests that in long tail languages the evolving agent may trade memory for
correctness or speed. Taken together, these results indicate that EvoCodeBench
can quantify not only endpoint accuracy gains from evolution, but also whether
those gains align with human efficiency distributions over the inference
trajectory.

![Refer to caption](x4.png) Figure 4. Performance comparison of evolving and
vanilla agents within-inference.

####  4.4.2. Within-Inference Evolution Trajectories

Figure [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4.1. Self-
Evolving Performance ‣ 4.4. Evaluation for Self-Evolving Agents ‣ 4. Empirical
Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-
Driven Coding Systems") illustrates how EvoCodeBench enables trajectory-level
evaluation of self-evolving coding agents. In the first row, the evolving
agent maintains consistently higher pass-rate trajectories across languages,
indicating that improvements persist as problems accumulate. In the second
row, the evolving agent exhibits substantially lower cumulative runtime, with
the widening gap suggesting compounding efficiency gains from fewer penalties
and faster solutions. In the third row, the evolving agent sustains higher
runtime-beats and memory-beats trajectories, showing that accepted solutions
become more competitive relative to humans as inference progresses. Together,
these signals complement endpoint metrics by revealing when and how within-
inference refinement improves correctness and efficiency.

##  5\. Conclusion

We introduced EvoCodeBench, a multilingual, execution based benchmark for
evaluating LLM based coding systems under a unified online judge protocol.
EvoCodeBench jointly measures error modes, resource efficiency, and human
referential competitiveness, enabling comparisons that remain meaningful
across high resource and long tail languages. Our results reveal systematic
performance degradation in long tail languages, distinct failure modes driven
by code level robustness and algorithmic inefficiency, and substantial
variation in structured output reliability. We further demonstrate that
EvoCodeBench supports within inference evaluation of self evolving agents by
exposing improvement trajectories in pass rate, cumulative runtime, and beats
metrics. We hope EvoCodeBench will facilitate more reliable evaluation and
drive progress toward coding agents that are robust across languages,
efficient under constraints, and competitive with human solutions.

##  Appendix A Code and Data Availability

All code and data will be publicly available upon acceptance of this paper,
including the benchmark query set, evaluation pipeline, backtest engine, and
supplementary scripts for reproducing the reported results.

##  Appendix B Motivation

The design of EvoCodeBench is driven by three complementary observations about
the current evaluation landscape for LLM-based coding systems. In this
section, we elaborate on each motivation in detail and explain how our
benchmark addresses the corresponding gap.

###  B.1. Evaluating Inference-Time Self-Evolution

A growing body of work explores how LLM-based agents can improve during
inference through iterative refinement, self-repair, and reflection (Madaan et
al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib21 "Self-refine:
iterative refinement with self-feedback, 2023"); Shinn et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib22 "Reflexion: language
agents with verbal reinforcement learning, 2023")). In the coding domain,
these systems refine candidate solutions by analyzing execution feedback,
diagnosing failure modes such as wrong answers or time-limit violations, and
producing revised implementations within a single problem-solving episode.
This inference-time self-evolution has been shown to substantially boost pass
rates, sometimes surpassing the performance of stronger base models operating
in a single-pass mode (Olausson et al.,
[2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib23 "Is self-repair a silver
bullet for code generation?")).

Despite the growing importance of such systems, existing code benchmarks are
not designed to characterize this behavior. They evaluate only the final
submitted solution and report a single correctness score, which collapses all
intermediate dynamics into one number. As a result, they cannot answer
questions such as: Does the system become more accurate as it iterates? Does
efficiency improve alongside correctness, or does the system trade runtime for
correctness? How many revision rounds are needed before gains saturate? These
trajectory-level questions are critical for understanding self-evolving
agents, yet they require benchmarks that expose per-iteration feedback
signals, including execution outcomes, runtime, memory, and partial-progress
indicators.

EvoCodeBench addresses this gap by recording the full sequence of submissions,
execution verdicts, and resource statistics across reflection and revision
steps. This enables trajectory-level analyses that separate one-shot
generation quality from inference-time adaptation gains, quantify the speed
and cost of improvement, and identify when self-evolution helps versus when it
introduces regressions. Our empirical results confirm that this design reveals
meaningful improvement dynamics. For example, the self-evolving agent achieves
pass-rate improvements of 10 to 27 percent relative to the vanilla agent, and
cumulative runtime decreases substantially as tasks accumulate, indicating
compounding efficiency gains that would be invisible under endpoint-only
evaluation.

###  B.2. Calibrating Performance Against Human Ability

Most code benchmarks report model performance in absolute units such as pass
rate or accuracy, which are difficult to interpret without an external
reference frame. A pass rate of 80 conveys limited information about whether
the system is approaching, matching, or exceeding typical human performance on
the same tasks. This interpretability gap is especially problematic as
frontier models approach high accuracy on popular benchmarks, making it
unclear whether remaining failures reflect fundamental limitations or merely
reflect difficult edge cases that also challenge human programmers.

Human-referenced evaluation provides a complementary perspective by locating
model performance within the empirical distribution of human submissions. On
platforms such as LeetCode, every accepted submission receives percentile-
based statistics that indicate the fraction of human solutions it outperforms
in runtime and memory. These runtime beats and memory beats metrics answer a
qualitatively different question from pass rate: not just whether the model
solves the problem, but how its solution compares to the solutions produced by
real human programmers on the same task and in the same programming language.

EvoCodeBench integrates these human-referenced signals as first-class
evaluation metrics. By reporting average runtime beats and average memory
beats alongside pass rate, our benchmark enables statements such as “the
model’s accepted solutions outperform 70 percent of human submissions in
runtime” or “the model achieves human-competitive memory efficiency in long-
tail languages despite lower pass rates.” These calibrated comparisons are
essential for interpreting the practical significance of benchmark scores and
for identifying settings where models are competitive with or superior to
typical human programmers, which has implications for deployment decisions and
trust in automated coding systems.

###  B.3. Assessing Cross-Language Robustness Under Long-Tail Usage

Existing code benchmarks are heavily concentrated on Python, which reflects
its dominant position in both the LLM training data distribution and the
developer ecosystem. According to the TIOBE Index for January 2026, Python
accounts for 22.61 percent of market share, while long-tail languages such as
Kotlin account for only 0.97 percent (TIOBE Software BV,
[2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib15 "TIOBE index")). This
skew has two consequences for evaluation. First, benchmarks that evaluate only
in Python cannot detect cross-language robustness issues, such as compilation
errors in statically typed languages or API misuse in less-represented
ecosystems. Second, the training data imbalance means that models are likely
to have seen far fewer examples of correct Kotlin or Go code, which can
translate into systematic performance degradation that single-language
benchmarks would miss entirely.

Several prior efforts have extended evaluation to multiple languages (Cassano
et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib19 "Multipl-e: a
scalable and polyglot approach to benchmarking neural code generation"); Ding
et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib20 "Crosscodeeval: a
diverse and multilingual benchmark for cross-file code completion"); Raihan et
al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#bib.bib5 "MHumanEval-a
multilingual benchmark to evaluate large language models for code
generation")), but they typically focus on translating existing Python
benchmarks rather than designing evaluation protocols that explicitly target
long-tail robustness. In particular, they rarely combine multilingual coverage
with efficiency metrics or human-referenced comparisons, which limits their
ability to diagnose whether performance gaps arise from algorithmic
deficiencies, implementation-level friction, or language-specific toolchain
issues.

EvoCodeBench includes five programming languages, spanning high-resource
(Python3, C++, Java), moderate-resource (Go), and long-tail (Kotlin) settings,
all evaluated under a unified online judge protocol with identical metrics.
This design enables systematic analysis of how pass rate, error profiles,
runtime, memory, and human-referenced beats shift as language resource
availability decreases. Our results confirm that this multilingual design
exposes robustness gaps that are invisible in Python-only evaluation:
compilation errors increase sharply in long-tail languages, overall pass rates
degrade systematically, and the gap between high-resource and long-tail
performance varies meaningfully across models. These findings motivate the
inclusion of long-tail languages as a standard component of code benchmark
design.

##  Appendix C Case Studies

###  C.1. Agent Construction Details

In the main paper, we introduced two standardized evaluation interfaces: a
lightweight coding agent and a self-evolving coding agent. This subsection
provides additional implementation details, including prompt templates, output
parsing rules, the submission pipeline, and the reflection and revision
procedure.

####  C.1.1. Coding Agent

The coding agent is designed to be minimally augmented so that observed
performance differences reflect the underlying model’s capabilities rather
than agent-level engineering. Its construction follows four steps.

Step 1: Prompt Construction. For each problem and target programming language,
the agent assembles a standardized prompt that consists of three components:
(1) the full natural-language problem statement, including constraints and
input–output examples; (2) any embedded images associated with the problem,
resolved to local assets; and (3) the language-specific starter code template
provided by the platform. These components are concatenated into a fixed-
format input string. The prompt explicitly instructs the model to return a
structured response containing two fields: a reasoning field for intermediate
analysis and a code field for the final solution. This format constraint
ensures deterministic parsing regardless of the model’s default output style.
An illustrative prompt is shown in Appendix Figure
[C.1.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10171v1#A3.SS1.SSS3 "C.1.3. Prompt Example
‣ C.1. Agent Construction Details ‣ Appendix C Case Studies ‣ EvoCodeBench: A
Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems").

Step 2: Model Inference. The assembled prompt is sent to the target LLM with
reasoning enabled by default and a maximum output token budget of 16,384
tokens. No system-level instructions, few-shot examples, or retrieval
augmentation are provided. The model generates its response in a single
forward pass without access to external tools, memory, or execution feedback.

Step 3: Deterministic Code Extraction. The agent parses the model’s response
and extracts the content of the code field using a deterministic extraction
rule. If the response does not conform to the expected format, the submission
is recorded as a response error. This strict parsing ensures that evaluation
failures due to format non-compliance are explicitly captured rather than
silently corrected.

Step 4: Online Judge Submission and Feedback Collection. The extracted code is
submitted to the LeetCode online judge for execution-based evaluation against
hidden test cases. The judge returns a verdict (Accepted, Wrong Answer, Time
Limit Exceeded, Memory Limit Exceeded, Compile Error, or Runtime Error), the
number of passed test cases, and, for accepted submissions, runtime in
milliseconds, memory usage in megabytes, and percentile-based runtime beats
and memory beats statistics computed against the distribution of human
submissions. All signals are recorded for downstream analysis.

####  C.1.2. Self-Evolving Coding Agent

The self-evolving coding agent extends the coding agent with a controlled,
within-inference reflection and revision loop. Its construction adds three
additional steps after the initial submission.

Step 5: Execution Feedback Analysis. After the initial submission (Steps 1–4),
the agent receives the judge’s verdict and diagnostic information. If the
submission is accepted, no further refinement is performed. If the submission
fails, the agent constructs a reflection prompt that includes: (a) the
original problem statement, (b) the previously submitted code, (c) the judge’s
verdict and error details (e.g., failed test case input and expected output
for wrong answers, or error messages for compile and runtime errors), and (d)
an explicit instruction to analyze the failure and propose targeted
improvements.

Step 6: Reflection and Revision. The model receives the reflection prompt and
generates an analysis of the failure, identifying potential root causes such
as unhandled corner cases, incorrect algorithmic logic, suboptimal time or
space complexity, or language-specific syntax issues. Based on this analysis,
the model produces a revised solution. The revised code is extracted using the
same deterministic parsing rule as in Step 3 and resubmitted to the online
judge.

Step 7: Iteration and Termination. Steps 5 and 6 are repeated for up to three
reflection and revision rounds (configurable). The loop terminates early if
any revised submission achieves an Accepted verdict. At each iteration, the
full execution feedback is recorded, enabling trajectory-level analysis of how
correctness, runtime, memory, and human-referenced beats evolve across
revision steps.

Key Design Constraints. Throughout the self-evolution process, only the
solution code is modified. The problem specification, prompt schema,
evaluation interface, and model parameters remain fixed. This ensures that
observed improvements are attributable solely to inference-time refinement
rather than changes in task formulation, prompt engineering, or external
augmentation. By constraining refinement to a fixed revision budget within a
single inference episode, the agent enables reproducible analysis of
improvement dynamics.

####  C.1.4. Self-Evolving Coding Agent Prompts

The self-evolving coding agent uses two types of reflection prompts depending
on the judge verdict: a _bugfix_ reflection when the submission fails and an
_optimization_ reflection when the submission is accepted but performance is
below a configurable threshold. The agent expects a structured JSON response
with three fields: analysis, improved_reasoning, and improved_code. The
reflection loop runs for at most three rounds and terminates early when the
solution is accepted with competitive performance (both runtime beats and
memory beats exceeding 65%). Throughout the process, only the solution code is
modified; the problem specification, prompt schema, and model parameters
remain fixed.

The reflection loop terminates when: (1) the maximum number of rounds (default
3) is reached; (2) the solution achieves Accepted with both runtime beats and
memory beats exceeding 65%; or (3) the model fails to produce a valid
reflection response. The agent always retains the best submission, preferring
Accepted solutions and, among those, the one with the highest runtime beats.

###  C.2. Accepted Test Cases

In this subsection, we present a representative selection of test cases where
the model successfully generated correct solutions, achieving an “Accepted”
status. These examples demonstrate the agent’s proficiency in handling a
diverse range of data structures and algorithmic paradigms, specifically
focusing on arrays, math, dynamic programming and graph theory. Through these
cases, we illustrate the model’s capability to interpret complex logic,
implement efficient algorithms (such as monotonic stacks and bitwise
operations), and satisfy strict execution constraints.

####  C.2.1. Case 1: Steps to Make Array Non-decreasing

In Case 1, the model addresses the problem “Steps to Make Array Non-
decreasing,” a task that requires sophisticated algorithmic reasoning. A naive
simulation of the removal process would result in a time complexity of
O​(N2)O(N^{2}), which violates the given constraints (N=105N=10^{5}). The
model successfully identifies the optimal approach using a monotonic stack,
demonstrating the ability to transform a simulation problem into a linear-time
O​(N)O(N) solution.

The generated explanation reveals a clear chain of thought: the model
correctly deduces that an element’s removal time depends on the maximum
removal time of the smaller elements it covers. By maintaining a stack of
(v​a​l​u​e,t​i​m​e)(value,time) tuples, the code effectively calculates the
”collision” logic required to determine when each element is removed. The
evaluation results confirm the solution’s correctness and efficiency, passing
all 87 test cases and outperforming 82.5% of Python3 submissions in runtime.
This case highlights the model’s capacity to handle complex state transitions
and data structure optimizations without human intervention.

Problem. Steps to Make Array Non-decreasing Tags: Array, Dynamic Programming,
Bit Manipulation Description: You are given a 0-indexed integer array nums. In
one step, remove all elements nums[i] where nums[i - 1] ¿ nums[i] for all 0 ¡
i ¡ nums.length. Return the number of steps performed until nums becomes a
non-decreasing array Example 1:  
Input: nums = [5,3,4,4,7,3,6,11,8,5,11] Output: 3 Explanation: The following
are the steps performed: Step 1: [5,3,4,4,7,3,6,11,8,5,11] becomes
[5,4,4,7,6,11,11] Step 2: [5,4,4,7,6,11,11] becomes [5,4,7,11,11] Step 3:
[5,4,7,11,11] becomes [5,7,11,11] [5,7,11,11] is a non-decreasing array.
Therefore, we return 3. Example 2:  
Input: nums = [4,5,7,7,13] Output: 0 Explanation: nums is already a non-
decreasing array. Therefore, we return 0. Constraints:  
∙\bullet 1 ¡= nums.length ¡= 10510^{5} ∙\bullet 1 ¡= nums[i] ¡= 10910^{9}

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,Y2xhc3MgU29sdXRpb246CiAgICBkZWYgdG90YWxTdGVwcyhzZWxmLCBudW1zOiBMaXN0W2ludF0pIC0+IGludDo=)

inference result:

1The problem asks for the number of steps to make an array non-decreasing by
removing elements ‘nums[i]‘ where ‘nums[i-1] > nums[i]‘ in each step. This can
be solved using a monotonic stack approach to track the ’time’ each element
takes to be removed. 2 3For each element ‘x‘ in ‘nums‘, we want to find the
nearest element to its left that is strictly greater than ‘x‘ (let’s call it
the ’killer’). However, the ’killer’ might be busy removing other elements
that are between it and ‘x‘. 4 5We maintain a stack of pairs ‘(value, time)‘,
where ‘time‘ is the step at which the ‘value‘ is removed. When we encounter a
new element ‘x‘: 61. We pop elements from the stack that are less than or
equal to ‘x‘. These elements cannot remove ‘x‘. 72. As we pop them, we keep
track of the maximum removal time ‘t‘ among them. This ‘t‘ represents the
number of steps required to clear out the elements between the potential
’killer’ (the current top of the stack) and ‘x‘. 83. If the stack is empty
after popping, it means there is no element to the left of ‘x‘ that is greater
than ‘x‘, so ‘x‘ will never be removed (‘time = 0‘). 94. If the stack is not
empty, the element at the top is the ’killer’ for ‘x‘. ‘x‘ will be removed at
step ‘t + 1‘. We then push ‘(x, t + 1)‘ onto the stack. 105. The answer is the
maximum removal time recorded across all elements. 11 12This approach ensures
that each element is pushed and popped from the stack at most once, resulting
in an O(n) time complexity and O(n) space complexity. 13 14# 15# @lc
app=leetcode id=2289 lang=python3 16# 17# [2289] Steps to Make Array Non-
decreasing 18# 19 20# @lc code=start 21class Solution: 22 def totalSteps(self,
nums: List[int]) -> int: 23 # stack will store pairs of (value,
time_to_be_removed) 24 stack = [] 25 max_steps = 0 26 27 for x in nums: 28 t =
0 29 # Pop elements that are smaller than or equal to current element x. 30 #
These elements are either already removed or will be ’blocked’ by x. 31 # We
need to find the max removal time among elements that x ’overtakes’. 32 while
stack and stack[-1][0] <= x: 33 t = max(t, stack.pop()[1]) 34 35 if not stack:
36 # No element to the left is greater than x, so x stays forever. 37
stack.append((x, 0)) 38 else: 39 # The element at stack[-1] is greater than x
and will eventually remove it. 40 # However, it must first remove all elements
that were processed 41 # between it and x (which took ’t’ steps). 42 t += 1 43
stack.append((x, t)) 44 max_steps = max(max_steps, t) 45 46 return max_steps

####  C.2.2. Case 2: Number of Effective Subsequences

In Case 2, the model tackles “Number of Effective Subsequences,” a problem
that demands a deep understanding of combinatorial mathematics and bitwise
operations. A brute-force approach iterating through all subsequences would
yield a time complexity of O​(2N)O(2^{N}), which is computationally
infeasible. The model successfully identifies that this is a counting problem
best solved using the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion (PIE) combined with Sum
Over Subsets (SOS) Dynamic Programming.

The model’s inference trace demonstrates a high level of abstraction: it
correctly formulates the problem as finding the number of subsets that
maintain the full bitwise OR sum, and then subtracting this from the total. It
employs an optimization technique—mapping the active bits of the total OR sum
to a compact range—to minimize the SOS DP state space to O​(d⋅2d)O(d\cdot
2^{d}), where dd is the number of set bits (at most 20). The evaluation
results (1041/1041 cases passed) and the high efficiency ranking (beating
71.26% of submissions) validate the model’s ability to implement complex
mathematical algorithms correctly.

Problem. Number of Effective Subsequences Tags: Array, Math, Dynamic
Programming Bit Manipulation Description: You are given an integer array
nums.The strength of the array is defined as the bitwise OR of all its
elements.A subsequence is considered effective if removing that subsequence
strictly decreases the strength of the remaining elements.Return the number of
effective subsequences in nums. Since the answer may be large, return it
modulo 10910^{9} \+ 7. The bitwise OR of an empty array is 0. Example 1:  
Input: nums = [1,2,3] Output: 3 Explanation: The Bitwise OR of the array is 1
OR 2 OR 3 = 3. Subsequences that are effective are: [1, 3]: The remaining
element [2] has a Bitwise OR of 2. [2, 3]: The remaining element [1] has a
Bitwise OR of 1. [1, 2, 3]: The remaining elements [] have a Bitwise OR of 0.
Thus, the total number of effective subsequences is 3. Example 2:  
Input: nums = [7,4,6] Output: 4 Explanation: The Bitwise OR of the array is 7
OR 4 OR 6 = 7. Subsequences that are effective are: [7]: The remaining
elements [4, 6] have a Bitwise OR of 6. [7, 4]: The remaining element [6] has
a Bitwise OR of 6. [7, 6]: The remaining element [4] has a Bitwise OR of 4.
[7, 4, 6]: The remaining elements [] have a Bitwise OR of 0. Thus, the total
number of effective subsequences is 4. Example 3:  
Input: nums = [8,8] Output: 1 Explanation: The Bitwise OR of the array is 8 OR
8 = 8. Only the subsequence [8, 8] is effective since removing it leaves []
which has a Bitwise OR of 0. Thus, the total number of effective subsequences
is 1. Constraints:

strictly decreases the strength of the remaining elements. Let $B$ be the
subsequence (set of indices) and $R = A \setminus B$ be the remaining
elements. The condition is $OR_{i \in R} (nums[i]) < S$. 33. Since every
$nums[i]$ is a submask of $S$, the OR of any subset $R$ is a submask of $S$.
Thus, $OR_{i \in R} (nums[i]) < S$ is equivalent to $OR_{i \in R} (nums[i])
\neq S$. 44. The number of effective subsequences is $2^n - f(S)$, where
$f(S)$ is the number of subsets $R \subseteq nums$ such that $OR_{i \in R}
(nums[i]) = S$. 55. By the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion (or Inverse Fast
Walsh-Hadamard Transform), $f(S) = \sum_{m \subseteq S}

####  C.2.3. Case 3: Remove Methods From Project

In Case 3, the model solves “Remove Methods From Project,” a graph theory
problem involving reachability analysis and constraint verification. The
solution requires a two-step logic: first, identifying the connected component
of “suspicious” nodes starting from node kk, and second, validating that no
external nodes invoke any node within this component.

The model correctly decomposes the problem, employing a standard Breadth-First
Search (BFS) to mark all reachable nodes from the source kk. Crucially, it
recognizes the necessity of a post-traversal validation step: iterating
through the edge list to detect if any “safe” node directs to a “suspicious”
node, which is the failure condition for removal. The implementation is highly
optimized, using an adjacency list for traversal and a boolean array for state
tracking, resulting in linear time complexity O​(V+E)O(V+E). The evaluation
confirms the efficiency of this approach, with the generated code
outperforming 99.38% of Python3 submissions.

###  C.3. Compile Error Resolution via Reflection Agent

This case exemplifies the capability of the Reflection Agent to handle
language-specific syntax errors that prevent code execution. The model
initially formulated a correct algorithmic strategy using Dijkstra’s algorithm
to solve the “Find Minimum Time to Reach Last Room I” problem. However, the
submission failed with a Compile Error due to an ambiguous import of
PriorityQueue in the Kotlin environment.

Upon receiving the error signal, the Reflection Agent did not merely
regenerate the code stochastically. Instead, it performed a targeted
diagnosis: it identified the conflict between the explicit import and the
environment’s implicit imports. Consequently, the agent refined the code by
adopting a wildcard import (java.util.*) and simplifying the data structure
from a custom data class to a primitive IntArray to reduce overhead. This
iterative self-correction process allowed the system to recover from a fatal
syntax error and achieve a fully accepted solution with competitive runtime
performance.
